items.title: Hosting panel for your own server
items.text:
Hostashi is a hosting control panel for a single Linux server. It runs PHP, Node.js, Python and static sites on nginx, with HTTPS, databases, backups and Git deploy, and it never needs root in the web process.

curl -fsSLO https://get.hostashi.com/install.sh
sudo bash install.sh --yes --panel-domain panel.example.com

Install guide Read the docs Source on GitHub

items.title: Everything a site needs, nothing it does not
Every kind of site
items.text: PHP in several versions side by side, Node.js, Python, static sites, reverse proxies, redirects and your own apps. WordPress in one step.

items.title: HTTPS without thinking
items.text: Let's Encrypt for every domain, wildcard certificates through your DNS provider, or your own certificate. HSTS and security headers per site.

items.title: Databases
items.text: MariaDB on the server, plus external MariaDB, MySQL and PostgreSQL servers. Size limits, import, export and a database tool in the browser.

items.title: Backups you can restore
items.text: Encrypted restic backups of files and databases to any SFTP server, up to hourly. Restore from the panel; backups of deleted sites stay until you remove them.

items.title: Git deploy and staging
items.text: Push to deploy with a webhook, build commands, atomic releases and rollback. Copy a site to staging and back.

items.title: Locked down by default
items.text: Each site runs as its own Linux user with limits. Firewall, fail2ban, virus scan, passkeys and TOTP, roles and an audit log.

items.title: Deploy from Git, roll back in a click
items.text:
Connect a repository from GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo or Bitbucket. Every deploy builds in a new release directory and goes live only when the build succeeds. The last releases stay, so going back is one click.

How Git deploy works

items.title: Backups that run while you sleep
items.text:
Choose a schedule and how many daily, weekly and monthly snapshots to keep. Restic encrypts every snapshot, and the panel warns you when a backup is overdue.

Set up backups

items.title: See who knocks, and let the right ones in
items.text:
The firewall rolls back changes you do not confirm, so you cannot lock yourself out. fail2ban bans are listed in the panel, and you can lift one without a shell.

Firewall and fail2ban

items.title: Made for
items.text:
• Agencies and freelancers who host their clients' sites on their own servers.
  • Admins who want a panel they can read, audit and change.
  • Anyone moving from CloudPanel: Hostashi scans the old server, copies sites and databases, and syncs once more before you switch DNS.

items.title: Not made for
items.text:
• Mail or DNS servers: use a mail provider and your registrar's DNS.
  • Billing, resellers or many servers from one panel.
  • Servers that already host websites: Hostashi installs on a fresh one.

items.title: Try it on a fresh server
items.text:
One script installs everything, and the panel greets you with a setup page.

Hostashi is built and maintained by Maki IT, which uses it on its own servers.

Install Hostashi Release notes

items.title: API tokens
items.text:
For: everyone with a panel account.

An API token lets a script, a monitoring system, a deploy job or the hostashi command line use the panel's API as you. You can have several tokens, one for each job, and each one has its own name, scopes, sites and lifetime. Revoke a token and only the job that used it stops working.

A token never gets more than your account: only the scopes your role can use and only the sites you can reach. If your account is disabled, its tokens stop working too.

items.title: Create a token
items.text:
1. Open Your account (your name at the bottom of the menu) and go to API tokens.
  2. Click New token and give it a name that says what uses it, for example "Uptime monitoring".
  3. Pick what the token may do. Only reading ticks the scopes that read, All but high risk everything except the scopes marked high risk, None clears the list. Pick high-risk scopes such as files:write or cron:write only if the job needs them.
  4. Leave Every site I can reach on, or untick it and pick the sites. A token limited to some sites works only on those sites; it cannot do what spans the server, such as creating a site, cloning one (a clone is a new site) or parking domains.
  5. Set how many days the token is valid, 1 to 365. Never expires is for a job you look after yourself; such a token works until you revoke it.
  6. Click Create token.

The panel then shows the token once. Copy it into your password manager or the secret store of your CI system and click I have saved it. Hostashi keeps only a hash and cannot show it again; if it is lost, revoke it and create a new one.

Creating, listing and revoking tokens needs a login in the browser. A token cannot create other tokens.

items.title: Use a token
items.text:
Send it in the Authorization header:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $HOSTASHI_TOKEN" https://panel.example.com/api/v1/sites

For the command line, pass it on stdin, or set HOSTASHI_URL and HOSTASHI_TOKEN (see Command line):

pass show hostashi/ci | hostashi login -token https://panel.example.com

hostashi login without -token creates a token for you through the browser, with the same choice of scopes, sites and lifetime. Those tokens are listed here as well, named after the computer.

items.title: Revoke a token
items.text:
Click the revoke button at the end of the row and confirm. Everything that uses the token gets 401 at once. Revoked and expired tokens stay in the list for reference; tick Show revoked and expired tokens to see them.

The list shows when and from which address each token was last used, so a token that nobody uses any more is easy to spot. A token that runs out within 30 days is marked Expires soon.

Every new token and every revocation is written to the audit log, and you get an email about a new token if you have an address set.

There can be up to 100 working tokens per account.

items.title: Limit where tokens are accepted from
items.text:
Admins can allow tokens only from known addresses, for example the office, the VPN and the CI runners. Open Firewall, go to the card API tokens and enter one IP address or CIDR range per line. An empty list accepts tokens from anywhere.

The list applies to the tokens of every account, at once. It is not a firewall rule, so it works without the Hostashi firewall and has no rollback; logins in the browser are not affected, so a wrong list cannot lock you out of the panel. A token used from another address gets 403 ip_not_allowed, and the attempt is written to the audit log.

The server itself, 127.0.0.1 and ::1, is always allowed, so the hostashi command on it keeps working whatever the list says. A token is still needed from there, so a local user of the server (for example a site's SSH account) gets no more than with any other address.

items.title: Access protection
items.text:
A site can let only some addresses in, block some addresses, or ask for a user name and password: for the whole site or only for some paths, such as the admin area of a CMS. nginx checks this before the site sees a request, for every file and page. You set it on the site's Security › Access tab.

For: everyone who can change the site.

items.title: IP rule
items.text:
1. Open the site and go to the Security › Access tab.
  2. Under IP rule, choose:
  3. Everybody may visit: no rule.
  4. Only these addresses may visit: every other address gets 403 Forbidden.
  5. Block these addresses: these addresses get 403 Forbidden.
  6. Enter the addresses or ranges, such as 203.0.113.7 or 203.0.113.0/24, one per line, at most 256.
  7. Click Save.

The tab shows your own address as the panel sees it. When your address is not on an Only these addresses list, the tab warns you before you save.

items.title: Password protection
items.text:
1. Under Users, add at least one user first (see below).
  2. Under Password, tick Ask for a user name and password.
  3. Choose For the whole site or Only for these paths. Paths start with /, one per line, at most 20. A path covers everything below it, in any upper or lower case: /wp-admin covers /wp-admin/ and /WP-Admin/users.php, but not /wp-administrator.
  4. Optional: under No password from these addresses, list addresses that never need the password, for example your office or an uptime monitor. The addresses of the server itself are refused, because every site on the server could connect from them.
  5. Click Save.

The browser shows its own dialog for the user name and password. After 10 wrong passwords in 10 minutes, fail2ban blocks the address for an hour, like after failed SSH logins.

The site's application no longer gets the browser's Authorization header on requests that need the password, so the password does not leak to the application. Where no password is asked, the header passes as before.

Each protected request costs nginx a few milliseconds to check the password. On a busy site, protect only the admin paths.

items.title: Users
items.text:
• Add user: enter a user name (letters, digits and . _ @ -, at most 64 characters). Choose Generate a strong password or Choose a password (12 to 72 characters). A generated password shows once: copy it before you leave the page.
  • New password (key icon): sets a new password for the user, generated or your own.
  • Remove (bin icon): asks once more, then removes the user. The last user stays while the password is on; switch the password off first.

A site has at most 50 users. The panel stores only a hash of each password; nobody can read a password back.

items.title: What always stays open
items.text: Let's Encrypt still reaches /.well-known/acme-challenge/, so certificates keep renewing. The panel's health check of the site also stays open.

items.title: Behind a CDN
items.text: Behind a CDN such as Cloudflare, every request comes from the CDN's addresses. Switch on Real visitor address first, or the IP rule and the addresses without a password see the CDN instead of the visitor.

items.title: Site types
items.text: Static, PHP, Node.js, Python, app and reverse proxy sites can use access protection. A redirect site has no Security › Access tab: nginx answers the redirect before it would check access. A site that becomes a redirect keeps its setting, but it takes effect only when the site becomes another type again.

items.title: Custom nginx snippets
items.text: A custom snippet on the Operations › nginx tab must not use allow, deny or satisfy while an IP rule is on, nor auth_basic, auth_basic_user_file or satisfy while the password is on. The panel refuses saving such a snippet, and it refuses switching on the rule while a snippet uses these directives.

items.title: Command line
items.text:
hostashi api sites get-access blog
hostashi api sites add-access-user blog name=office
hostashi api sites set-access blog password:=true 'paths:=["/wp-admin"]'
hostashi api sites set-access blog ipMode=allow 'ips:=["203.0.113.0/24"]'
hostashi api sites set-access-user-password blog office
hostashi api sites delete-access-user blog office

set-access replaces the whole setting: fields you leave out are switched off. Without password a user name and password stops being asked. add-access-user and set-access-user-password without password= generate one and print it once.

items.title: Application profiles and hardening
items.text:
An application profile tells the panel what runs on a static or PHP site, such as WordPress or Laravel. The profile brings hardening rules: nginx answers requests for files that should never be public with 404, before the site's files or PHP see them. You choose the profile when you create a site and can change it later on the site's Security › Hardening tab.

For: everyone who can change the site.

items.title: The profiles
items.text:
Profile Needs PHP Serves Rules besides blocked dumps and backups Static site – htdocs none Generic PHP any htdocs none WordPress 7.4 htdocs no PHP in wp-content/uploads, xmlrpc.php blocked, wp-login.php rate limited WooCommerce 7.4 htdocs as WordPress Laravel 8.2 htdocs/public none Symfony 8.2 htdocs/public none Shopware 6 8.2 htdocs/public none TYPO3 8.2 htdocs/public no PHP in fileadmin and typo3temp Drupal 8.3 htdocs/web no PHP in sites/default/files

The folder a profile serves only applies to new sites. Changing the profile of an existing site never touches its files or its web root.

items.title: Choose a profile for a new site
items.text: On Hosting → Sites → New site, pick the Application of a PHP site below the PHP version. The panel refuses a PHP version older than the profile needs. Without a choice, a PHP site gets Generic PHP, and a static site always starts with Static site.

items.title: Change the profile or its rules
items.text:
1. Open the site and go to the Security › Hardening tab.
  2. Choose a Profile. Its rules fill the form, and its notes appear below it.
  3. Change the rules if the site needs it, for example clear xmlrpc.php from Blocked files when the WordPress app or Jetpack needs it.
  4. Click Save profile and rules. nginx uses the new rules right away.

The panel stores only what differs from the profile. When a later Hostashi version changes a profile, a site keeps its own changes and gets the rest. The badge Changed from the profile shows that the site has changes; Use the profile's rules drops them.

items.title: See the server block
items.text: Show the server block below the rules shows the nginx configuration the site gets with the chosen profile and the rules in the form, before you save them. It changes as you edit the form. The panel renders it with the same templates as the server, but it is read only and saves nothing. Paths below /placeholder, such as the web root, the PHP socket and the certificate, stand for the server's own paths. Password protection shows its rules but never the users or their password hashes. Custom snippets that point into the site's home are left out with a note. A site in maintenance or switched off is shown as it is served when it is back online. Everyone who can see the site can open it; the API route is POST /api/v1/sites/{name}/profile/preview.

items.title: The rules
items.text:
Rule What nginx does Block database dumps, backups, logs and editor copies 404 for files ending in .sql, .sql.gz, .sql.bz2, .sql.xz, .sql.zst, .dump, .bak, .backup, .old, .orig, .save, .swp, .swo, ~, .log, .env or .ini, anywhere below the web root Blocked folders 404 for everything in these folders Blocked files 404 for these files Folders without PHP (PHP sites) a .php file in these folders never runs, it gets 404; other files are served as before Rate limited PHP files (PHP sites) at most 12 requests per minute per address, 10 more at once, then 429

Paths are relative to the web root, one per line, at most 20 per list, for example wp-content/uploads. They may contain letters, digits, ., _ and -, separated by /.

Hidden files and folders such as .git, .env or .htaccess are always blocked with 404, whatever the profile. /.well-known stays open, so Let's Encrypt and other checks keep working.

items.title: Own profiles
items.text:
Admins can make their own profiles, for example a WordPress profile that also blocks readme.html, or a static profile that serves htdocs/dist. An own profile has the same values as a built-in one and no nginx text.

For: admins. Everyone who can create or change a site can choose an own profile.

items.title: Copy a profile
items.text:
1. Go to Hosting → App profiles.
  2. Click Copy next to the profile to start from.
  3. Give the copy a Name (up to 40 lower-case letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter; built-in names are taken) and a Title.
  4. Change the values: the site type, the lowest PHP version, the web root folder, the page cache preset, the hardening rules, suggested cron jobs and the checklist.
  5. Click Add profile.

Own profiles appear after the built-in ones on New site and on the site's Security › Hardening tab. Static profiles are offered for static sites.

items.title: Change or delete an own profile
items.text:
Change saves new values. Sites that use the profile get its new hardening rules right away and keep their own changes. The web root folder only applies to sites created afterwards. The name cannot change, and the site type cannot change while sites use the profile.

Delete works only while no site uses the profile; the panel names the sites that still do. Give them another profile on their Hardening tab first. Built-in profiles cannot be changed or deleted.

Every change of an own profile is in the audit log as profile.create, profile.import, profile.update or profile.delete.

items.title: Export and import as YAML
items.text:
Export downloads a profile, built-in or own, as hostashi-profile-<name>.yaml:

version: 1
name: agency-wp
title: Agency WordPress
type: php
minPhp: "8.2"
hardening:
  configFiles: true
  noPhpDirs:
    - wp-content/uploads
  denyFiles:
    - xmlrpc.php
    - readme.html
  limitFiles:
    - wp-login.php
pageCache: wordpress
checklist:
  - Install the agency's plugin set.

To import, click Import YAML, choose the file or paste it, and click Import profile. The panel refuses a file without version: 1, with fields it does not know (such as nginx text), with more than one document or larger than 64 KiB, and every value it would refuse in the form. The name must not be taken: edit it in the text field to import a profile a second time.

From the command line, the same works through hostashi api; a token needs the scope settings:write to change profiles:

hostashi api sites export-profile agency-wp > agency-wp.yaml
jq -Rs '{yaml: .}' agency-wp.yaml | hostashi api sites import-profile -d -

Own profiles do not carry nginx snippets. For extra nginx rules, an admin adds a custom snippet on the site's Operations › nginx tab.

items.title: Install WordPress
items.text:
Any active PHP site can get WordPress in one step. The panel creates a database and its user, then WP-CLI downloads and installs WordPress as the site's user. The PHP site's own PHP version runs it.

  1. Open the site and go to the App › Web tab.
  2. Under WordPress, fill in the site title, the language, the admin user and the admin email. Do not call the admin user admin: bots try that name first.
  3. Leave Generate a strong admin password on, or set your own of 12 to 128 characters.
  4. Click Install WordPress.

The web root must be empty; WordPress installs only into an empty folder. The database is called <site>_wp, with - in the site name turned into _; if that name is taken, the panel uses <site>_wp2 and so on. It counts for the site's databases like any other, see Databases.

A generated password is shown once, together with the login address, the user and the database. Copy it before you click I have saved it; the panel does not keep it. A lost password can be reset from the WordPress login page.

The install takes about a minute. The card shows its progress and, at the end, the log of WP-CLI. The log stays readable afterwards under Operations › Logs › WordPress install, see Site logs. A site whose profile was Generic PHP gets the WordPress profile. The installed WordPress has file editing in the dashboard switched off (DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT).

After the install, a Shell key gives you the wp command for WP-CLI on the site, with the site's PHP version.

items.title: When the install fails
items.text: The card shows the error and the log. The database stays. If the web root is empty, the form is there again; otherwise empty it in the file manager or over SSH, or use Reinstall WordPress. Delete the database on the Databases tab if you no longer need it.

items.title: Reinstall WordPress
items.text:
The card looks at the web root itself. It says WordPress is installed when it finds wp-config.php or wp-includes/version.php, also for a WordPress you installed by hand. If you delete WordPress in the file manager, the install form comes back.

Reinstall WordPress replaces everything in the web root with a new WordPress:

  1. Back up the site first, see Backups. A reinstall cannot be undone.
  2. Click Reinstall WordPress, fill in the form as for a new install, and type the site's name to confirm.
  3. Click Reinstall WordPress again.

The install run empties the web root first, as the site's user, then installs WordPress into a new database (<site>_wp2 if <site>_wp is taken). Themes, plugins, uploads and every other file in the web root are gone. The old WordPress database, the one wp-config.php names, is deleted once the install started, but only if it belongs to the site and has a quick install's name (<site>_wp to <site>_wp9). Any other database stays; delete it on the Databases tab if you no longer need it.

items.title: Audit log
items.text:
Hostashi writes every change made in the panel or through the API to an audit log: who did it, when, what it was and what it concerned. Failed logins and rejected API tokens are in it too. Entries cannot be changed or deleted, not even by an admin.

For: admins. Managers and users do not see the audit log.

items.title: View the log
items.text:
1. Open Audit log in the Administration part of the menu.
  2. The newest entries come first. Show older entries loads the next 50.
  3. Narrow the list with the filters above the table:
  4. Action: one action, such as site.create, or a whole group, such as site.* (all).
  5. Account: the exact username. An account that was deleted since keeps its name in the log and shows (deleted).
  6. Target: part of what the action concerned, usually a site, database or account name.
  7. IP address: the exact address the change came from.
  8. From and To: days in your browser's time zone, both included.

The filters are part of the address, so you can bookmark or share a filtered view.

The IP address column shows the address of the browser or API client that made the change. Work the panel does by itself, such as scheduled jobs, has no address.

The Details column shows what the panel recorded with the action. For an update it lists each field that changed, with the old value struck through and the new value next to it. Passwords, keys and cron commands never appear: the log only says that they changed.

items.title: Export
items.text:
CSV and JSON at the top right download the log with the filters you set, oldest entry first, including the IP address and the changes of each entry. CSV opens in a spreadsheet; JSON suits scripts. Each export is itself written to the log, with its format and filters.

In the CSV file a cell that starts with =, +, - or @ gets a leading ', so that a spreadsheet does not run a crafted username as a formula.

items.title: API
items.text:
The same data is available to API tokens with the scope audit:read, only for admins:

  • GET /api/v1/audit with the optional query values action, actor, target, ip, since, until (RFC 3339), limit (1 to 200) and before (the next value of the previous page).
  • GET /api/v1/audit/actions lists every action in the log.
  • GET /api/v1/audit/export?format=csv or format=json with the same filters.

items.title: Backups
items.text:
For: panel admins.

Hostashi backs up every site's files and every database once a day with restic, encrypted, to an SFTP server. Restores never touch the live site.

Any SSH server that offers SFTP and accepts key login works: a Hetzner Storage Box, a NAS, or another Linux server. The account only needs write access to the backup directory; it does not need a shell.

items.title: Set up the target
items.text:
1. Create an account on the SFTP server for the backups. On a Hetzner Storage Box, turn on SSH access in its settings (a sub-account limited to one directory works well).
  2. Open Server → Backups → Target and schedule and enter the user, the host (DNS name or IP address), the port and a directory. The port is usually 22; a Storage Box uses 23. The directory is relative to the login directory, or absolute when it starts with /. It is created on the first run.
  3. The panel shows a public key. Add it to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys of that account (on a Storage Box also possible in Hetzner's console).
  4. Under Host key, fetch the server's SSH host key and compare the fingerprint with the server's own, for example ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub on that server, or the fingerprints your provider publishes. Backups start only after you confirm it.
  5. Under Run backups, choose how often: once a day, or every 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 or 12 hours. Once a day starts at a random time in the window between the two hours. Shorter intervals start at a fixed random minute after each of those hours, counted from midnight. All times are server time. A backup that is still running when the next one is due skips that one, so two backups never overlap.
  6. Choose how many hourly, daily, weekly, monthly and yearly snapshots to keep. For each hour, day, week, month and year, the newest snapshot is kept, up to these counts. Hourly only matters when backups run more than once a day; hourly and yearly are 0 by default.

Back up now runs a backup right away; it runs in the background.

items.title: Keep the keys outside the server
items.text:
The backups are encrypted with a repository password. Restoring on a new server also needs the panel key. Print both once and store them in a password manager:

sudo hostashi backup key show

Without them, the backups are useless if the server is lost. They are never shown in the panel or the API.

items.title: Data check
items.text: Once a month Hostashi reads part of the stored data back and checks it, a different part each month. Data check parts sets how much: each month 1 of that many parts is read; 0 turns it off. Status shows the last backup and the last data check.

items.title: Restore files
items.text:
1. Under Snapshots, choose the site.
  2. Pick a snapshot and choose restore.
  3. Hostashi writes it into a new folder restore-<time> in the site's home. Nothing in the live site changes.
  4. Copy what you need from there into place, with SFTP or the file manager, and delete the folder afterwards. It counts against the site's disk limit.

items.title: Restore a database
items.text:
Each database has its own snapshots in the same list. Restoring one writes its dump (<database>.sql, or .dump for PostgreSQL) into a restore-<time> folder of the site. The panel then offers Import into a new database: the dump goes into a new database, and the old one stays as it is. Check the new database, then point the site's configuration to it.

You can also import the dump into an existing database yourself, see Databases.

On the command line, the same is hostashi backup restore SITE SNAPSHOT.

items.title: Backups of deleted sites
items.text:
Deleting a site does not delete its snapshots. Administrators find them under Snapshots in the site list, in the group Deleted sites.

  1. Choose the deleted site.
  2. Under Restore into, choose an existing site, for example a new site you created for it.
  3. Restore a snapshot. Files go into a new folder restore-<time> in the home of that site; a database dump can then be imported into a new database of that site, as above.

If you create a new site with the name of a deleted one, the new site only shows the snapshots taken since it was created. The older ones are listed as (earlier site) under Deleted sites and can be restored into the site of the same name.

items.title: Delete the backups of a deleted site
items.text:
The snapshots of a deleted site stay until you delete them. Below the snapshots of a deleted site, type its name and choose Delete backups of …. The next backup run removes them; Back up now removes them at once. Until that run, Keep backups takes it back. The space is freed by the next weekly cleanup of the repository. For an earlier site, only the snapshots from before the current site was created are deleted.

To remove them automatically, set Deleted sites (days) under Keep snapshots. A backup run then removes the snapshots of a deleted site once its newest snapshot is older than that many days. 0, the default, keeps them until you delete them. Earlier sites of a reused name are never removed automatically. The status shows what the last run removed.

On the command line: hostashi backup deleted lists deleted sites with snapshots, hostashi backup deleted SITE their snapshots, and hostashi backup restore-deleted SITE SNAPSHOT TARGET restores one into the site TARGET. hostashi backup delete-deleted SITE marks the backups of a deleted site for removal by the next run, and hostashi backup keep-deleted SITE takes that back.

items.title: Moving from CloudPanel
items.text:
For: panel admins.

Hostashi can take over the sites of a CloudPanel server: their domains, files, databases, PHP settings, cron jobs, SSH keys and checked nginx directives. The move goes from the old server to a new server with Hostashi; the old server keeps running until every site is switched, and is turned off afterwards.

Open Administration → CloudPanel import. The page walks through these steps.

items.title: 1. Connect the old server
items.text:
1. Under Old server, enter its address and SSH port. Prefer the IP address: DNS names move during the migration.
  2. The panel shows an authorized_keys line. Add it to root's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the old server. The key is locked: it can only read files over SFTP and reach the old server's database port, nothing else.
  3. Under Host key of the old server, run the fingerprint command on the old server and compare. Confirm the matching key. Nothing is copied before that.

items.title: 2. Give database access
items.text:
To copy databases, Hostashi needs a read-only database user on the old server. Under Database access, the panel shows the SQL for the old server; run it there as the database root. Files are copied without it.

A new password replaces the old one. If you make a new one, run the new SQL on the old server too.

items.title: 3. Scan the old server
items.text:
1. Download the hostashi archive for the old server's architecture (linux_amd64 or linux_arm64) from the releases, check it against SHA256SUMS and unpack it on the old server.
  2. Run the scan command shown on the page as root:
./hostashi cloudpanel scan -json -full > hostashi-scan.json

It only reads the CloudPanel configuration and changes nothing. 3. Upload hostashi-scan.json under Scan reports.

The report lists every site and what can be taken over. Show plan shows what Hostashi would create for a site and which entries it skips.

items.title: 4. Move each site
items.text:
Do this site by site.

  1. Create the site. The site gets the old domains, its PHP version and settings, cron jobs and SSH keys (as SFTP only; switch a key to Shell afterwards if needed). It has no certificate yet; HTTPS follows after the DNS switch. If the old site sent www.example.com to example.com (or the other way round), the new site gets the same www redirect; other redirect hosts become redirect domains of the site. A site the scan found WordPress in gets the WordPress application profile: xmlrpc.php is blocked, PHP never runs in wp-content/uploads and wp-login.php is rate limited. If the site needs xmlrpc.php, for example for Jetpack, allow it on the site's Security › Hardening tab.
  2. Files and databases. Start the import. The old files land in cloudpanel-import in the site's home, and the web root stays as it is. Map each old database to a database of the site (create those on the Databases page first). The dumps are loaded into the databases shortly after.
  3. Custom nginx. Directives from the old site are shown once for checking. Check every line, then save them; they are active right away.
  4. Final sync. Shortly before the DNS switch, run the import again. Then choose Use imported files as web root.
  5. DNS switch. The panel shows the records to set for every domain: point them to this server and remove all other A and AAAA records. It checks what the domains resolve to and, once they point here, gets the certificate and turns on HTTPS. Lower long DNS TTLs to 300 seconds a day before, so the switch is quick.

items.title: Node.js, Python and reverse proxy sites
items.text:
• A Node.js site becomes a Node.js site. It gets the newest Node.js line installed on this server (install one on the Node.js page first), or another line you choose. Its app gets a new port in PORT and stays stopped until you set the start command on the site's App › Web tab, after the final sync. The old process manager, for example pm2, is not taken over.
  • A Python site becomes a Python site. It gets the newest Python line installed on this server (install one under Python versions first), or another line you choose; the old version is not scanned. Hostashi makes ~/.venv. The app gets a new port in PORT and stays stopped. After the final sync, install the packages into ~/.venv over SSH (the plan names requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when the scan found one), then set the start command on the site's App › Web tab. The old process manager is not taken over.
  • A reverse proxy site becomes a reverse proxy site to the same target. It has no Linux account here, so there are no files, databases, cron jobs or SSH keys to move: skip step 2. A target on the old server itself, such as 127.0.0.1, cannot be taken over. An https target's certificate is checked; turn the check off in the site's settings if the target uses a self-signed certificate.

items.title: 5. Clean up
items.text:
When every site is switched:

  • Forget old server in the panel, and remove the authorized_keys line and the read-only database user on the old server.
  • Turn the old server off.

CloudPanel's own panel users and its backups are not taken over: invite the people again (Users and roles) and set up backups on the new server.

items.title: Command line
items.text:
For: server admin. Every command runs on the server as root, for example with sudo, unless it says otherwise.

Most work is done in the panel. The command line is for what the panel cannot do for you: the first login, getting back in, checks and emergencies.

items.title: Getting in
items.text: Command What it does hostashi setup-token Prints the one-time token for the first login. hostashi user recover [-public-url URL] NAME Removes the password and second factors of account NAME, enables it and prints a new invitation link. See Recovery.

items.title: Using the API from the command line
items.text:
These commands work as any user and on any machine, not only on the server. They talk to the panel's API with an API token, so your role, the token's scopes and the audit log apply as in the panel.

Command What it does hostashi login [URL] Logs in through the browser. It prints a link and a code such as WDJB-MJHT. Open the link in a browser where you are logged in to the panel (with a passkey or a password and second factor), check that the panel shows the same code and the name of your computer, pick what the token may do and approve. The command then stores the token in ~/.config/hostashi/credentials.json (only readable by you). URL is the panel's address, for example https://panel.example.com; on the server itself it defaults to http://127.0.0.1:8080. hostashi login -token [URL] Reads an existing API token from stdin instead, for scripts (see below). hostashi whoami Shows the account, its role and the token's scopes. hostashi api Lists the areas of the API, such as sites, databases or backups. hostashi api AREA Lists the commands of an area with their arguments. hostashi api AREA COMMAND -h Explains a command: the request it sends, the token scope it needs and its fields. hostashi api AREA COMMAND ARGS Runs it and prints the answer as JSON, or a download as it is. hostashi logout Removes the stored token. It stays valid until it expires; revoke it in the panel under Your account → API tokens if it may have leaked.

For example, with the token in a password manager:

pass show hostashi | hostashi login -token https://panel.example.com

Every operation of the API is a command of hostashi api, so anything the panel can do through its API, the command line can do as well. Arguments after the command are, in this order:

  • the names in the route, such as the site: hostashi api sites get blog
  • fields as key=value; numbers, true/false and comma-separated lists are converted to the field's type: hostashi api limits set-site blog preset=small
  • any JSON value as key:=JSON: hostashi api limits set-site blog 'custom:={"memory":1073741824}'
  • the whole body with -d JSON, -d @FILE or -d - for stdin
  • a file for an upload as key=@FILE: hostashi api pages create-status name=sorry kind=maintenance file=@sorry.html

Commands marked "panel only" refuse API tokens, for example creating tokens; use the panel for them (see API tokens).

HOSTASHI_URL and HOSTASHI_TOKEN override the stored login, for example in CI jobs. Plain http:// is only accepted for the server itself (127.0.0.1, ::1, localhost), so that a token never crosses a network unencrypted.

Approve only a login you started yourself: whoever started it gets a token for your account. A code is valid for ten minutes.

items.title: Tab completion
items.text:
The installer sets up tab completion for bash, zsh and fish. In a new shell, hostashi si and Tab completes to hostashi site, and hostashi api sites create and Tab shows the fields of that command. Completion knows the commands, their flags, the areas and commands of hostashi api and the keys of hostashi site limits. It needs no login and does not ask the panel, so it does not complete names of sites or databases.

For bash, the package bash-completion must be installed (it is on most servers). On another machine, or for a shell the installer does not know, load the script yourself:

source <(hostashi completion bash)        # in ~/.bashrc
source <(hostashi completion zsh)         # in ~/.zshrc, after compinit
hostashi completion fish | source         # in ~/.config/fish/config.fish

items.title: Checks
items.text: Command What it does hostashi doctor Checks the server and every site without changing anything. Exit code 3 if a check failed, 0 otherwise. -json prints the result as JSON. hostashi ping Checks that the agent answers. hostashi version Prints the version.

items.title: Services
items.text:
These commands go through the panel's API like hostashi api, also as root on the server: log in once with hostashi login first. Your role and the token's scopes (services:…, system:…) decide what works, and every change is in the audit log. Naming the action on the command line counts as the confirmation the panel asks for.

Command What it does hostashi service list Lists the services with their state and automatic restarts. -json prints JSON. hostashi service ID [SITE] ACTION Runs an action, for example hostashi service nginx reload or hostashi service php blog restart. Only the actions of the service catalog work. hostashi system info Shows the hostname, time zone, clock, uptime and a pending reboot as JSON. hostashi system timezones Lists the time zones the server knows. hostashi system timezone ZONE Sets the time zone, for example hostashi system timezone Europe/Berlin. hostashi system hostname NAME Sets the hostname and updates /etc/hosts (see System settings). hostashi system reboot HOSTNAME Reboots the server; the hostname confirms it.

items.title: Sites
items.text:
site create, site delete, site list and site limits go through the panel's API and need hostashi login. site files talks to the agent and needs root on the server.

Command What it does hostashi site list Lists the sites with their type, pool, state and domains. hostashi site create NAME DOMAIN[,DOMAIN...] [POOL] Creates a static site with its domains, for example hostashi site create blog blog.example.com,www.blog.example.com. Change it afterwards in the panel or with hostashi api. hostashi site delete NAME Deletes a site with its files, databases and virtual host. hostashi site files NAME Starts the file manager of a site and prints its socket. The panel does this by itself; the command is for checks. hostashi site limits NAME Shows the preset and the limits of a site. hostashi site limits NAME preset=PRESET Gives the site a limit preset. hostashi site limits NAME KEY=VALUE ... Changes single limits, for example hostashi site limits blog memory=536870912 cpu-priority=high. Values you leave out stay as they are; 0 means no limit.

site limits goes through the panel's API, like in Site → Limits: it needs hostashi login and a token with limits:read (and limits:write to change). The keys are memory and disk (bytes), inodes, tasks, php-workers, cpu-priority (low, normal or high), cpu-quota (percent of one CPU), db-size (bytes, only warns) and db-connections.

items.title: Storage pools
items.text:
A storage pool is an extra volume for site homes, for example a provider volume for large sites. Hostashi never formats or mounts a volume. You prepare it first:

Before you format: check the device twice. Formatting erases everything on the volume, and mkfs does not know whether you still need it. Before step 1, run lsblk -f and cat /etc/fstab and make sure the device is the new, empty volume: it has no mount point, no label or UUID that /etc/fstab still uses, and is not where /home lives. Hypervisors and cloud consoles may attach a volume under a name that an earlier disk had (/dev/sdb), so go by size and serial (lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,SERIAL,LABEL,UUID,MOUNTPOINTS), not by name.

If the volume replaces an old one, remove or comment out the old line in /etc/fstab and run systemctl daemon-reload. A line whose device is gone makes systemd wait 90 seconds for it at every login below that mount point, and without nofail the next boot stops in emergency mode. hostashi doctor reports such lines (system.fstab).

  1. Create an ext4 or XFS file system on the volume. For disk limits per site, create it with project quota: mkfs.ext4 -O quota,project -E quotatype=prjquota /dev/... (an existing, unmounted ext4 volume: tune2fs -O project,quota -Q prjquota /dev/...). XFS needs nothing at this step.
  2. Add it to /etc/fstab by UUID (from lsblk -f, not /dev/sdX) with nosuid,nodev,nofail and, for disk limits, prjquota, for example UUID=... /srv/vol1 ext4 nosuid,nodev,nofail,prjquota 0 2, then run systemctl daemon-reload and mount it.
  3. Leave it empty (lost+found is fine).

Without project quota a pool works, but its sites get no disk limit. The agent switches on the enforcement of the limits on every pool that counts usage, at its start and when a pool is added, so no quotaon is needed. hostashi pool list and hostashi doctor show the quota state of each pool: enforced, counting (limits are not enforced, doctor reports a failure) or off.

Command What it does hostashi pool add [-default] NAME PATH Adds the mounted volume at PATH as pool NAME. It refuses, with the reason, a path that is not a mount point, not ext4 or XFS, not mounted with nosuid,nodev, not in /etc/fstab, not empty, inside a system directory or overlapping another pool. With -default, new sites land on it when they name no pool. hostashi pool list Lists the pools with their path, number of sites and quota state; the default pool ends with default. hostashi pool rename NAME NEWNAME Gives a pool a new name. Its path, its sites and their files stay where they are. Goes through the panel's API (needs hostashi login). hostashi pool default NAME Makes a pool the default for new sites that name no pool. Goes through the panel's API (needs hostashi login). hostashi pool remove NAME Removes a pool without sites that is not the default. Then you can unmount the volume.

The panel shows the same under Server → Storage pools, where admins can also rename a pool and make it the default. Adding and removing a pool stay on the command line, because they need a mounted volume on the server.

hostashi doctor fails a pool whose volume is not mounted or whose marker is missing, and warns when a pool's volume is mounted without nosuid,nodev or has no /etc/fstab entry. It also checks every block device in /etc/fstab: a device that does not exist fails without nofail and warns with it. While a volume is missing, its sites do not start and cannot be changed; mount it and restart hostashi-agent.

A site gets its pool when it is created and stays there. Its databases stay in MariaDB's own directory.

items.title: Databases
items.text:
These commands go through the panel's API, like Site → Databases, and need hostashi login with the databases:… scopes.

Command What it does hostashi db list Lists the databases with their site and users. hostashi db create SITE NAME Creates a database for a site. hostashi db delete NAME Deletes a database and its users. hostashi db user create DATABASE USER Creates a database user. Reads the password from standard input; an empty line generates one and prints it once. hostashi db import DATABASE FILE Loads a dump into a database. FILE is relative to the site's home and ends in .sql or .sql.gz. hostashi db export DATABASE FILE Writes a dump of a database into the site's home. hostashi db user password USER Sets a new password for a database user. Reads it from standard input; an empty line generates one and prints it once. hostashi db user delete USER Removes a database user.

items.title: Backups
items.text:
These commands go through the panel's API and need hostashi login, except backup key show, which only root on the server can run.

Command What it does hostashi backup get Shows the backup settings, the public key and the state as JSON. hostashi backup set Sets the target, retention and time window. Reads the settings as JSON from standard input. hostashi backup hostkey Confirms the host key of the backup server. Reads one public key line from standard input. hostashi backup start Starts a backup now. hostashi backup status Shows the state of the last backup. hostashi backup restore SITE SNAPSHOT Restores a snapshot into a new folder restore-<time> in the site's home. Nothing existing is overwritten. hostashi backup restore-status ID Shows the state of a restore. hostashi backup deleted [SITE] Lists deleted sites that still have snapshots, or the snapshots of one. A site name that a newer site took again shows the snapshots from before that site was created. Administrators only. hostashi backup restore-deleted SITE SNAPSHOT TARGET Restores a snapshot of a deleted site into a new folder restore-<time> in the home of the existing site TARGET. Administrators only. hostashi backup delete-deleted SITE Marks all snapshots of a deleted site, or of an earlier site of a reused name, for removal by the next backup run. Administrators only. hostashi backup keep-deleted SITE Takes the mark back before the next backup run. Administrators only. hostashi backup key show Prints the backup repository password and the panel key. Store them outside the server: without them, backups cannot be restored on a new server.

items.title: Moving from CloudPanel
items.text:
Command What it does hostashi cloudpanel scan Run on the old CloudPanel server. Shows which sites can be moved, changes nothing.

The rest of the move is done in the panel. A full guide follows.

items.title: All commands
items.text:
hostashi help prints every command, including the ones the panel and the system services use internally.

The package also installs a manual page with the same list, so man hostashi works on the server. It is made from the same text as hostashi help and changes with it.

items.title: Cron jobs
items.text:
For: everybody who can open a site, including users.

A cron job runs a command on a schedule, as the site's Linux user, inside the site's limits. Open the site's App › Cron tab.

items.title: Add a cron job
items.text:
Field Meaning Schedule five cron fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week), for example */15 * * * * for every 15 minutes, or @hourly, @daily, @weekly, @monthly Command one line, run by the shell in the site's home, for example php htdocs/wp-cron.php Time limit in minutes the job is stopped when it runs longer Priority (nice) 0 to 19; higher numbers leave more CPU to the site itself

The list shows the last and the next run of each job and how the last run ended.

items.title: See the output of a run
items.text:
Click the result under Last run, or choose More → Show output. You see what the command wrote to standard output and standard error in its last run: at most the last 200 lines, as long as the server's system journal keeps them. Copy copies the text. Everybody who can see the site's cron jobs can see their output, so do not let a job print passwords.

Beside the output, Last runs lists up to the last 10 runs with their start, result and duration. Click one to see what that run wrote. How far back the list goes depends on how long the system journal keeps entries.

On the command line: hostashi api cron list-job-runs SITE ID lists the runs, and hostashi api cron get-job-output SITE ID run=RUN shows the output of one; without run= it is the last run.

items.title: Run, pause and delete
items.text:
• Run now starts a job right away; its result shows up under Last run.
  • More → Change opens the job's form.
  • More → Pause keeps the job but stops its schedule. It then runs only when started by hand.
  • More → Delete removes it.

While a site is disabled, its cron jobs do not run.

items.title: Tips
items.text:
• Use the full path below the home or a path relative to it; the job starts in the home folder.
  • For WordPress, turn off its built-in cron (define('DISABLE_WP_CRON', true);) and run php htdocs/wp-cron.php every 5 to 15 minutes instead.

items.title: DNS accounts
items.text:
By default Let's Encrypt checks a domain over HTTP: it fetches a file from port 80 of the server the domain points to. With a DNS account, Hostashi can prove the domain over DNS instead (DNS-01): it writes a short-lived TXT record through the API of your DNS provider. That helps when

  • port 80 is closed or the site sits behind a proxy that does not pass the check through,
  • you want the certificate before the domain points to this server, for example when you move a site,
  • and later for wildcard names such as *.example.com, which Let's Encrypt only issues over DNS.

Hostashi does not run DNS itself. It only creates and deletes _acme-challenge TXT records at your provider.

For: admins. Managers and users see which check a site uses but cannot switch it to DNS, because DNS can get certificates for names that do not point to this server.

items.title: Providers
items.text: Provider What Hostashi needs Cloudflare An API token with Zone: Read and DNS: Edit on the needed zones only. Never the global API key. Hetzner A read/write API token of a Hetzner Cloud project. Use a separate project that holds only DNS zones: a token of a project with servers can delete them. Tokens of the old DNS Console do not work. INWX Username and password, and the shared secret if the account uses two-factor login. Use a sub-user with DNS rights only, if your account offers one.

items.title: Add an account
items.text:
1. Go to Administration › DNS accounts and click Add DNS account.
  2. Choose the provider, give the account a name and list its zones, one per line, for example example.com.
  3. Enter the credentials and click Add DNS account.

Hostashi then checks the access: it creates and deletes a test record _acme-challenge.<zone> in each zone. The list shows Can write, or Failed with the provider's answer. A failed check does not stop you from saving; fix the token or the zones and click Check.

The credentials are stored encrypted and are never shown again, not even to admins. To change them, edit the account and tick Replace the credentials; otherwise they stay as they are.

Each zone belongs to one account. A zone may be a subdomain, for example acme.example.net.

items.title: Which account a domain uses
items.text: For each domain, Hostashi looks at the name the TXT record must have: _acme-challenge.<domain>, or where a CNAME there points. The account whose zone covers that name, the longest one if several do, writes the record. A domain that no account covers cannot use DNS: the panel says which challenge name is missing.

items.title: Recommended: a separate zone for the challenges
items.text:
A token that can edit your real zones can also change your MX or A records. You can avoid that by delegating only the challenge records to a zone that exists for nothing else:

  1. Create a zone, for example acme.example.net, at a provider Hostashi supports, and add a DNS account for only that zone.
  2. Once per domain, add a CNAME at the domain's own DNS, wherever it is:
_acme-challenge.example.com.  CNAME  example.com.acme.example.net.
  1. Hostashi follows the CNAME and writes the TXT record into acme.example.net.

The domain's own DNS can then stay at any provider, also one Hostashi does not support, and the token has no rights on your real zones.

items.title: Switch a site to DNS
items.text:
On the site's Domains & HTTPS › HTTPS tab, under Check by Let's Encrypt, choose DNS: a TXT record through a DNS account. Hostashi refuses the switch if a domain of the site has no account. The current certificate stays; its renewals, Renew now and a new certificate after a domain change go over DNS from then on.

For the panel's own address, the same choice is on the System page under Panel certificate.

A DNS certificate takes longer than one over HTTP, usually one to three minutes: Hostashi waits until the zone's name servers show the record before Let's Encrypt checks it.

items.title: Remove an account
items.text: Remove asks first. Hostashi refuses to remove an account, or to take a zone away from it, while a site or the panel gets its certificate over DNS through it. Switch those to HTTP or give their zones to another account first.

items.title: API
items.text:
• GET /api/v1/dns-providers lists the providers and their fields.
  • GET and POST /api/v1/dns-accounts, GET, PUT and DELETE /api/v1/dns-accounts/{id}, POST /api/v1/dns-accounts/{id}/check. Tokens need dns_accounts:read or dns_accounts:write; only admins can create such tokens.
  • PUT /api/v1/sites/{name}/tls/challenge and PUT /api/v1/panel/tls/challenge with {"challenge": "dns"} or {"challenge": "http"}.

A domain without an account answers 422 no_dns_account; removing an account in use answers 409 dns_account_in_use. Every change goes into the audit log; the credentials never do.

On the command line, for example:

hostashi api dns-accounts add label="INWX main" provider=inwx zones=example.com,acme.example.net 'credentials:={"username":"dns-user","password":"…"}'
hostashi api sites set-tls-challenge shop challenge=dns

items.title: Database limits
items.text:
Every site has two values for its local databases, next to its disk space and memory: a size at which Hostashi warns, and how many connections each of its database users may open at the same time. They come from the site's limit preset and can be changed per site.

For: administrators, who edit the presets, and managers, who change the limits of a site. Everyone who can open a site sees its values.

items.title: The values
items.text:
Field What it does small medium large Database size Warning threshold for all local databases of the site together, in GiB 2 GiB 5 GiB 10 GiB Database connections Connections at the same time, per database user (MAX_USER_CONNECTIONS) 20 40 80

The preset values are estimates for typical WordPress sites. Unlimited switches a value off.

items.title: Change them
items.text:
• One site: open the site, go to the Operations › Limits tab and choose another preset, or Custom and enter the values under Database.
  • A preset: open Limit presets in the menu and edit the preset. Every site that follows the preset gets the new values.

items.title: Database size
items.text:
The size is the data and the indexes of the site's tables, as MariaDB reports them. For InnoDB tables this is an estimate, so it can differ from the files on disk by some percent. Hostashi measures it at most every five minutes. The Databases tab shows the size of each database, the Operations › Limits tab the sum against the threshold.

The size is only a warning. Nothing stops a database from growing past it, because a hard stop would break the site at once: no logins, no orders. Hostashi warns in three places:

  • the Operations › Limits tab of the site, from 80 percent,
  • the Health page, check Database size: a warning from 80 percent and an error from 95 percent,
  • an email from 90 percent, in the category Disk space of the email notifications, at most once a day.

When the warning comes, look for data the site no longer needs (old logs, sessions, post revisions, cached data in tables), or raise the threshold if the server's disk has room. Databases live in /var/lib/mysql and do not count against the site's disk space.

items.title: Database connections
items.text:
A login above the limit fails with MariaDB error 1226 (User has exceeded the 'max_user_connections' resource). The limit keeps one site's runaway script from taking every connection of the server. It counts per database user, so a site with two users can open twice as many connections.

If a site legitimately needs more, raise the value on its Operations › Limits tab. Hostashi applies the new value to every database user of the site at once; connections that are already open stay open.

The temporary users of the web database tool (Adminer) and of import and export jobs keep their own fixed limits.

items.title: External database servers
items.text: Databases on external database servers are not measured and get no connection limit: Hostashi does not manage the storage or the connections of a server it does not run.

items.title: Databases
items.text:
For: everybody who can open a site, including users.

Every database belongs to one site. By default databases live in the server's own MariaDB; admins can add external servers (see below).

items.title: Create a database
items.text:
1. Open Hosting → Databases → New database.
  2. Choose the site, the database name and the user name (lowercase letters, digits and _, starting with a letter).
  3. If there are several database servers, choose one. A database stays on the server it is created on.
  4. After creating, the panel shows the password once. Copy it into the site's configuration, for example wp-config.php.

Hostashi does not store database passwords and cannot show them again. If one is lost, set a new one on the database's page: the old password stops working at once, so update the site's configuration right after.

In the site's configuration, use localhost as the database host for the server's own MariaDB. For an external server, use the host name shown in the server list.

items.title: Import and export
items.text:
• Import: on the database's page, under Import or export, choose Import a file. MariaDB and MySQL take .sql or .sql.gz, PostgreSQL also .dump (pg_dump custom format).
  • My computer: pick the file. The panel uploads it into hostashi-imports/ in the site's home, imports it and removes it again. While it is there it counts towards the site's disk space.
  • The home of site …: enter the path of a file already in the site's home, for example one uploaded with SFTP or the file manager.
  • Export: enter the file to write, relative to the home. An existing file is never replaced.

items.title: Browse and edit the data
items.text:
If the web database tool is installed, Open in Adminer opens the database in a new browser tab. Hostashi creates a temporary database user for it; that user and its connections end after the session length you choose. No password reaches your browser.

The top bar in Adminer shows when the session ends. +30 min opens the panel in a new tab, where one click extends the session; the Adminer tab shows the new time when you go back to it. Logout in Adminer opens the panel, where one click ends the session: the temporary user is removed and its connections close. The database's page in the panel lists the open sessions with the same two actions.

items.title: Delete a database
items.text: On the database's page, Delete database removes it together with its users. This cannot be undone. Databases of a site are also deleted when the site is deleted.

items.title: External database servers
items.text:
For: admins. Under Hosting → Databases → Database servers, add a MariaDB, MySQL (8.0 or newer) or PostgreSQL server that the panel creates databases on:

  • Give it a name for the panel, the host name or address, the port and an administrator account. For MariaDB and MySQL it needs CREATE, DROP, CREATE USER and GRANT OPTION; for PostgreSQL a role with CREATEDB and CREATEROLE, not a superuser.
  • The panel stores that administrator password encrypted. It is the only database password Hostashi keeps.
  • Use TLS with the server's CA certificate. Unencrypted connections work, but only inside a private network you trust.
  • For PostgreSQL, allow only this server's address in its pg_hba.conf.

New databases go to the server marked as default. Removing a server from the panel changes nothing on the server itself.

See also Database limits.

items.title: Domains and HTTPS
items.text: For: panel admins and managers. Users cannot change domains or certificates, because a domain is a claim on a name that other customers might need.

items.title: Point the domain to the server
items.text:
Before you add a domain to a site, create DNS records at your DNS provider:

Record Name Value A example.com and www.example.com the server's IPv4 address AAAA the same names the server's IPv6 address, if it has one

Hostashi does not run DNS. Let's Encrypt checks each name over HTTP on port 80, so the records must resolve to this server and port 80 must be open. With a DNS account, admins can switch a site to a check over DNS instead.

items.title: Change the domains of a site
items.text:
On the site's Domains & HTTPS › Domains tab, edit the list: one domain per line, the first one is the primary domain. The site keeps its name, Linux user, files, databases, backups and settings; only the names it answers to change.

Redirect domains answer every request with a permanent redirect (301) to the primary domain, path and query included. Use them for old names after a move, or for extra names that should not show the site themselves. They stay on the site's certificate, so their DNS records must keep pointing to this server; remove a name from the list once you no longer need it.

A domain can belong to one site or parked domain only, and never be the panel's own host name.

items.title: Wildcard domains
items.text:
Reverse proxy and redirect sites can also answer for every subdomain: add *.example.com after the primary domain. A request for any name below example.com that no other site serves then reaches this site. Typical uses are an app that serves its customers under their own subdomain, or a redirect of every old subdomain to the main site.

  • Names of other sites, parked domains and the panel's address always win. With *.example.com on one site and www.example.com on another, www.example.com goes to its own site. The Domains tab lists such names.
  • *.example.com does not cover example.com itself; list both if the site should answer for both.
  • The wildcard also matches deeper names such as a.b.example.com, but a wildcard certificate covers only one level, so those get a certificate error over HTTPS.
  • The wildcard cannot be the primary domain or a redirect domain, and other site types cannot have one. To change the type of such a site, remove the wildcard first.
  • A redirect site may send *.example.com to https://www.example.com when another site serves www.example.com. A target the site would answer itself is refused, as it would loop.
  • DNS: create a wildcard record such as A *.example.com that points to the server.

Let's Encrypt checks a wildcard only over DNS. Create the site without HTTPS, then either choose DNS as the check on the HTTPS tab (admins, with a DNS account for the zone) and turn HTTPS on, or upload an own wildcard certificate. Both tabs warn when no DNS account has a zone for the wildcard.

items.title: When the change takes effect
items.text:
• Site on HTTPS with Let's Encrypt, new names: the change waits until a certificate for all new names is there, usually less than a minute. Until then the site stays on HTTPS with its current domains. If a new name has no working DNS record yet, nothing changes: the tab shows the error, and the panel tries again within the hour. You can Try again now, Change now without HTTPS (the site is served over HTTP until the certificate is there; with HSTS on, browsers that know the site refuse that) or Cancel change. The new names are reserved for this site while the change waits.
  • Everything else (site on HTTP, own certificate, or the certificate already names every domain): at once.

items.title: Change the primary domain
items.text:
Change primary domain does the common move in one step: enter the new domain, choose whether its www name is added too, and whether the old domain (and its www name) becomes a redirect domain. The form shows the domains after the change before you save.

The panel does not change what the site itself stores: addresses in the database (for WordPress run wp search-replace 'https://old.example.com' 'https://example.com' --all-tables over SSH, after a backup), values such as APP_URL in the app's environment or config files, and DNS. The form lists these with the command for your domains.

items.title: Redirect to or from www
items.text:
Most sites should answer under one name only, either example.com or www.example.com, and send visitors on the other name there. Choose this in the www redirect card on the same tab:

  • No redirect: every domain shows the site. This is the default.
  • Redirect to the name without www: www.example.com sends visitors to example.com.
  • Redirect to the www name: example.com sends visitors to www.example.com.

The redirect is a permanent one (301) and keeps the path and query, so www.example.com/shop?page=2 goes to example.com/shop?page=2. With HTTPS on, it goes straight to HTTPS in one step, and HSTS and the security headers are sent on the redirect too.

Both names must be domains of the site. If one is missing, the card offers a button such as Add www.example.com; it adds the name like the domain list above does, so create its DNS record first. With HTTPS on, the site is served over HTTP until the new certificate also names it. Hostashi never adds the other name on its own, because a name without a DNS record would stop the certificate for the whole site.

The setting works on every pair of a domain and its www name, so a site with example.com, www.example.com, example.de and www.example.de redirects both pairs. Other domains of the site, such as shop.example.com, are not touched. Redirect sites do not have this card: they send every name to their target anyway.

items.title: HTTPS
items.text:
The switches and the certificate are on the Domains & HTTPS › HTTPS tab. With HTTPS with a Let's Encrypt certificate on, Hostashi gets a certificate for all domains of the site, renews it on its own and redirects HTTP to HTTPS. Sites are served with HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.

If the certificate cannot be issued, the site page says why, for example a domain that does not point to the server. Hostashi tries again within an hour. Fix the DNS record and wait, or use Renew now on the certificate card.

items.title: HSTS
items.text: HSTS: browsers use only HTTPS for this site tells browsers to never use plain HTTP for the domain again. Turn it on only once HTTPS works: browsers remember it for a year, even if you turn it off later.

items.title: Own certificate
items.text:
If you get certificates from another CA, use the certificate card on the same tab:

  • Upload certificate: paste or upload the certificate, the chain (optional) and the private key (PEM, no passphrase; RSA with at least 2048 bits, or ECDSA P-256 or P-384). The key passes through your browser and the panel.
  • Create CSR: Hostashi creates the key on the server and shows a certificate signing request. Give it to your CA and upload the certificate you get back. The key never leaves the server.

Hostashi checks that the key matches, the chain is complete, the certificate is valid and covers every domain of the site before it goes live. Own certificates are not renewed automatically: the panel warns 30 and 7 days before they expire.

items.title: Email notifications
items.text:
Hostashi can send invitations, security notes and notifications by email. It does not run a mail server: it hands every message to an SMTP relay you already have, such as your own mail server or a sending service.

Email is off until an admin sets up a relay. Without it everything works as before: the panel shows invitation links to copy, and problems show up on the overview and the Health page.

items.title: Set up the relay
items.text:
For: admins.

  1. Open Email in the Administration part of the menu.
  2. Enter the relay:
  3. Host and Port of the SMTP server.
  4. Encryption: STARTTLS (usually port 587) or TLS (usually port 465). Hostashi never sends mail without encryption and always checks the server's certificate. For a relay with a certificate from your own CA, paste that CA under CA certificate (PEM).
  5. Username and Password, if the relay wants a login. Hostashi sends them only inside the encrypted connection and keeps the password encrypted with the server key. The page never shows it again; leave the field empty to keep it.
  6. From address and From name: the sender of every email, for example panel@example.com and Hostashi.
  7. Reply-to, optional.
  8. Save, then enter your own address under Send to and send a test email. The page shows the relay's answer, for example 535 5.7.8 authentication failed, if something is wrong.

Examples of relay settings (check your provider's documentation for the current values):

Relay Host Port Encryption Your own mail server mail.example.com 587 STARTTLS Amazon SES (eu-central-1) email-smtp.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com 587 STARTTLS Brevo smtp-relay.brevo.com 587 STARTTLS Postmark smtp.postmarkapp.com 587 STARTTLS

Deliverability is the relay's job. Set up SPF and DKIM for the sender domain at your provider, otherwise the emails may end up in spam. Hostashi does not sign messages itself.

Links in emails point to the panel's own address (the --panel-domain of the installer), never to whatever address a request came in on.

items.title: Your email address
items.text:
For: every account.

On Your account → Email, enter your address. Hostashi sends a link to it; the address is used only after you open that link (within 24 hours). Changing the address sends a note to the old one. When an admin invites you with an address, accepting the invitation confirms it.

items.title: What Hostashi sends
items.text:
Account emails go to your own confirmed address and cannot be switched off:

  • an invitation or a reset link from an admin,
  • a second factor added or removed, a passkey added or removed, a new API token,
  • your email address changed.

Notifications are about the server and sites. Switch them on or off on Your account → Notifications. They are on by default for admins and off for everyone else; Git deploys are off for everyone until switched on. You only get notifications about what your role can see: backups and server checks only go to admins; managers get those of every site, users those of their own sites.

Notification When Backups A backup failed or did not save everything. Once per run. Certificates A renewal failed (at most once a day), or a certificate expires in 14 or in 3 days. Server checks Once a day, when the checks on the Health page find errors. Also once per new Hostashi version, when the server does not install it by itself (--auto-update). Services A service is down (systemd gave up restarting it) or crashed 3 times within 15 minutes, or the panel cannot reach the Hostashi agent for about 3 minutes. Another email when it runs again. Server services go to admins; PHP and the object cache of a site also to managers and users of that site. Malware scan A malware scan of a site flagged files it had not reported before. Once per run, with up to 10 paths and signatures; files you marked as false positives are not reported again. Git deploys A Git deploy of a site failed: its build, its switch to the new release, or its start. Once per run, with the commit, who started it and the error; the log stays in the panel. A failed rollback sends none, as the panel shows it right away. PHP versions Once a week per site, when a site uses a PHP version that loses security fixes within 60 days or already has. Disk space A disk of the server or a site's disk limit is 90 percent full or more, or a site's databases reach 90 percent of their warning size. At most once a day.

items.title: Language
items.text:
Emails are plain text in English or German. Each recipient gets the language set under Your account → Appearance → Language; Follow the browser means English, because an email has no browser to follow. An invitation goes to an account that has no setting yet, so it is in the language of the admin who sent it. Times are in the server's time zone (Server → System). The texts of the server checks are translated too, in the disk space, database size, PHP version and Hostashi update emails as in the daily list of failed checks. Error messages from programs such as restic, nginx or the ACME client stay in English.

At most 10 emails per recipient and 100 per server go out each hour. Above that, notifications wait for the next hour; account emails are always sent.

Hostashi itself sends these emails, so it cannot report an outage of the panel, of the whole server or of its network. Use a check from outside for that, for example an uptime monitor that opens your sites.

items.title: When email does not arrive
items.text:
• The Health page and the overview show Email with a warning when messages failed in the last 24 hours, with the relay's last answer.
  • Hostashi tries again after 1, 5, 15 and 30 minutes and then every hour or two, for up to 24 hours. A permanent rejection (a 5xx answer, for example an unknown recipient) is not retried.
  • Send a test email on the Email page to see the relay's answer right away.
  • Invitation and reset links are always shown on the Users page as well, so you can copy them by hand.

Email is not a secure channel: anyone with access to a mailbox can open an invitation link in it. Links work once and only for 24 hours, and admins and managers still need a second factor.

items.title: File manager
items.text: Every site has a Files › File manager tab between "Domains & HTTPS" and "PHP". It shows the site's home folder (/home/<site>); the web root is htdocs.

items.title: What you can do
items.text:
• Browse folders. The folder is part of the address, so the browser's back button and bookmarks work.
  • Upload files and whole folders with Upload, or by dragging them onto the table. Large files go up in parts of 8 MiB; a cut connection resumes.
  • Download a file, or a folder or a selection as a ZIP.
  • Create folders and empty files with New. Rename, move, copy, change the mode and delete one entry from its ⋯ menu, or several at once by ticking them; renaming happens right in the row.
  • Scan a selection for viruses while the virus scan is on.
  • Change the mode (for example 644 or 755). setuid, setgid and the sticky bit cannot be set.
  • Extract a ZIP into a folder. Files that exist already are kept unless you choose to replace them.
  • Edit text files up to 1 MiB: click the file's name to open it in the code editor, with syntax highlighting, find and replace (the magnifier or Ctrl+F), a full screen switch and saving with Ctrl+S. A file too large for the editor downloads when you click its name. If someone changed the file since you opened it, saving is refused instead of overwriting their change.

Deleting asks once and lists what it deletes. There is no recycle bin; backups are the way back.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
What Limit entries shown in one folder 20,000 (use SFTP for more) file size in the editor 1 MiB, UTF-8 text ZIP extraction 100,000 entries and 10 GiB unpacked folder and file names 255 bytes

Symlinks are shown with their target but never followed: you cannot open, download or edit through them. Use SFTP for them.

items.title: Who can use it
items.text: The file manager needs the permissions files:read (browse, download) and files:write (everything that changes files). Admins and managers have both for every site; a user has them for the sites assigned to them. API tokens get them only when you select them. Every change and every download is written to the audit log.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
The panel never touches the site's files itself. It talks to a small helper, hostashi-files@<site>.service, which systemd starts when the tab is used. The helper runs as the site's Linux user, inside the site's resource limits, with no network and no access outside the home folder. It stops 5 minutes after the last request. Files it writes belong to the site's user, just as with SFTP.

hostashi doctor checks that the helper's units are installed, that no helper runs as root, and that none has run for more than a day.

To give all files of a site back to its user and reset their modes at once, use Reset file permissions below the file manager.

items.title: Firewall
items.text:
For: panel admins.

Hostashi runs its own firewall (nftables). It lets in SSH, the websites and the panel, and drops everything else. Outgoing traffic is not limited. If your provider has a firewall in front of the server as well, that one still applies: open a port there too.

Open Server → Firewall. The tab Firewall holds the rules below and the allowlist for API tokens; the tab Blocked addresses shows what fail2ban blocks (see Blocked after failed logins).

items.title: What is always open
items.text: Ports 80 and 443 (TCP, and UDP for HTTP/3) are always open for the sites and cannot be closed in the panel. SSH (22) and the panel port (8443) are open to everyone until you set an allowlist.

items.title: Allowlists for SSH and the panel
items.text:
Under Allowlists, enter the addresses or networks (for example 203.0.113.7 or 198.51.100.0/24) that may reach SSH or the panel. Everyone else is dropped. The page shows your address as the panel sees it, so you do not lock yourself out.

If the panel runs on port 443 under its own host name, its allowlist is checked by nginx instead (see Install).

Where API tokens are accepted from is set on the same page, in its own card; see API tokens.

items.title: Open more ports
items.text: Under Opened ports, add a port or a range (3000 or 6000-6010), the protocol and, optionally, the addresses it is open to.

items.title: Every change rolls back unless you confirm it
items.text:
A wrong rule could cut you off, so each change is tested first:

  • Panel access changed: your browser checks that the panel still answers and confirms on its own.
  • SSH allowlist changed: the panel asks you to open a new terminal and log in over SSH. Keep the session you have open until that works, then choose SSH works, keep the rules.
