items.text: On Overview → Availability, Disable shows a maintenance page to every visitor and stops the site's PHP. Files, databases and settings stay. Enable brings it back.

items.title: Your own maintenance and parking pages
items.text: Under Maintenance pages you can upload your own page: one .html file, or a .zip file with index.html at the top and its CSS, JavaScript, images and fonts. Write %%DOMAIN%% in the HTML where the visitor should see the domain they opened, for example <p>%%DOMAIN%%</p>. The web server puts in the visited domain in lower case, such as www.example.com; internationalized domains appear in their ASCII form (xn--…). The preview shows example.com. The placeholder is replaced in HTML files only, not in CSS or JavaScript.

items.title: Delete a site
items.text:
On Overview → Delete site. This deletes the site with its files and databases and cannot be undone. Backups stay until they expire.

To keep the domains answering, you can park them in the same step: choose the domains to park and a parking page. Domains you leave out are free afterwards. See Parked domains.

items.title: Staging and copies
items.text:
Copy site creates a new site from an existing one. You get a copy of its files, of its databases on this server and of its settings. A staging copy is meant for trying changes, such as a WordPress or plugin update, a new theme or another PHP version. You test on a separate domain with real content, and the live site stays as it is.

It is in the Actions menu of the site header (Copy site…), which opens the card on the site's Overview. Only admins and managers see it.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
1. Point the copy's domain at the server first, for example staging.shop.example.com. The copy then gets its certificate right away.
  2. Open the live site and choose Actions → Copy site…. Name and domain come filled in as staging-<site> and staging.<first domain>. Change them if you like, and choose another storage pool if there is one.
  3. Leave Staging copy checked. Check Put in maintenance while copying if the live site must not change halfway through the copy, for example a shop that takes orders. Then click Create staging copy.
  4. Save the login that is shown now. A staging copy asks every visitor for it. Hostashi shows the password only once; you can set a new one later under Security › Access.
  5. The copy shows its progress on its own Overview tab: first the files, then the databases, then the configuration. When it is done, the copy is ready on its domain.
  6. Test on the copy. When you are happy with the result, make the same change on the live site, for example by running the same update there.

    7. There is no "copy to live". Copying the database back would overwrite everything the live site collected in the meantime, such as orders, comments and customer accounts.

items.title: What is copied
items.text:
Copied Not copied all files of the home folder, except .ssh and the Git deploy cache domains and certificates: the copy has its own every database on this server, as a new database with its own user and password databases on external database servers: an application that uses one is not configured, and its copy stops with a message site type, PHP version, PHP settings, web options and nginx snippets the page cache: it starts empty limits, security headers, visitor address, access rules (without the password users) the object cache's content: the copy gets a new, empty one the application profile and its hardening rules Git deploy and its webhook cron jobs: paused in a staging copy SSH keys the app's environment variables which accounts with the role user may manage the site

Before it starts, Hostashi checks that the storage pool has room for the files plus 10 % and the server has room for the databases plus 10 %.

items.title: The application's configuration
items.text:
The copy has to use its own database and its own domain, otherwise it would write into the live site's database:

  • WordPress: Hostashi sets DB_NAME, DB_USER and DB_PASSWORD in wp-config.php. For a staging copy it also sets WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE to staging. Then it replaces every link to the live domains (with and without www, http and https) with the copy's domain in the database (wp search-replace) and flushes the cache. Plugins and themes are not loaded while it does this.
  • Laravel: Hostashi sets APP_URL, and either DB_URL or DB_DATABASE, DB_USERNAME and DB_PASSWORD in .env. It also removes the cached configuration bootstrap/cache/config.php.
  • Symfony: Hostashi changes user, password and database in DATABASE_URL, in .env.local when that file sets it, else in .env. A compiled .env.local.php stops the copy: delete it on the source or run composer dump-env again after the copy.
  • Other applications: the copy's card lists what to change by hand: the database names, the site's own address and live services such as mail or payments.

The application profile decides which of these applies (see Application profiles). If the configuration names a database that was not copied, the step fails rather than letting the copy use the live data.

items.title: A staging copy
items.text:
A staging copy is marked Staging in its page head. It differs from a plain copy in four ways:

  • Password: the whole site asks for the generated login (Access protection).
  • Search engines: every answer carries X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow. The switch is on the App › Web tab, card Search engines.
  • Cron jobs: paused, so nightly jobs do not send mail or import orders twice. Turn single jobs back on under Cron jobs.
  • Refresh: it can be refreshed from its source.

Before you test: the application's own mail settings are copied too. A shop on the copy can therefore send real order mails to real customers, and environment variables may hold live API keys, for example of a payment provider. Switch these to test settings first.

items.title: Refresh from the source
items.text:
On the staging copy, Refresh from copies the live site's files and databases into the copy again. Domain, login, databases and users of the copy stay; everything changed on the copy is replaced. Type the copy's name to confirm. Here too you can put the live site in maintenance while it is copied.

While a copy or refresh runs, neither site can be copied or refreshed again.

items.title: Maintenance during the copy
items.text: The files and the databases are copied one after the other. Anything the live site writes in the meantime, such as a new order, can therefore end up in the copied database without its uploaded files, or the other way round. With Put in maintenance while copying the live site shows its maintenance page (see Sites) until files and databases are copied, and Hostashi turns the maintenance off again by itself, also when the copy fails. A site that was already in maintenance stays in it.

items.title: When something fails
items.text: The copy's card shows the reason. A first copy that fails is deleted again together with its new databases, and the reason stays in the audit log under site.clone.failed. A refresh that fails keeps the copy, marked as failed, and you can run it again.

items.title: Who can use it
items.text:
Admins and managers. API tokens need the scopes sites:write and databases:write. Every copy and refresh is written to the audit log.

From the command line:

hostashi api sites clone shop name=staging-shop domain=staging.shop.example.com staging=true
hostashi api sites get-clone staging-shop
hostashi api sites refresh-clone staging-shop

items.title: System settings
items.text:
Hostashi shows the server's hostname, time zone, clock and uptime, changes the hostname and the time zone, and reboots the server (ADR-0060). The page also holds the panel's own certificate and its real visitor address.

For: admins. Managers and users do not see the page.

Open System in the Server part of the menu.

items.title: Server
items.text: The first card shows the hostname, the time zone, the server's clock and whether it is synchronized, and the uptime. Reboot needed appears when installed updates wait for a reboot, with the packages that asked for it. The server never reboots by itself.

items.title: Hostname
items.text:
Use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. A full name such as web2.example.org works too, up to 64 characters. The panel's address and the sites do not change.

Hostashi sets the name through systemd and also:

  • points the 127.0.1.1 line in /etc/hosts to the new name, so sudo and local lookups keep working;
  • writes /etc/cloud/cloud.cfg.d/90-hostashi-hostname.cfg if cloud-init is installed, so it does not set the cloud's server name again at the next boot.

items.title: Time zone
items.text:
Type to search the list of zones the server knows. Before you save, the hint shows what the server's clock would read.

  • The sites' cron jobs follow the new time zone at once.
  • MariaDB uses it after its next restart (Services, MariaDB, restart).
  • PHP keeps its own date.timezone (see PHP settings).

items.title: Updates
items.text:
Shown on servers set up from the hostashi package. The card shows the installed Hostashi version and the newest one apt saw in the Hostashi repository (apt fetches the list once a day). The versions link to their release notes.

Node.js and Python patches shows the package hostashi-runtimes: newer patch releases of the pinned Node.js and Python lines, published as signed data in the suite runtimes of the Hostashi repository and installed by unattended-upgrades every day, independent of the switch below (ADR-0077). The agent then installs the new release with its checksum check. Not set up means the installer has not run since the package came; the Health page says so too.

The switch Automatic updates applies at once and is recorded in the audit log:

  • On: unattended-upgrades installs new Hostashi versions together with the daily security updates. Each update keeps a copy of the panel database first. Hostashi writes /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/53hostashi-auto-update for it, the same file as the installer option --auto-update.
  • Off: new versions wait for sudo apt upgrade. The Health page and an email say when one is out.

A later run of the installer without --auto-update leaves the switch as it is.

items.title: Panel certificate
items.text:
Shown when the panel has its own host name (see Install). It works like a site's certificate (see Domains and HTTPS): Let's Encrypt renews it by itself, or you upload an own certificate or create a CSR. The panel's certificate cannot be deleted.

The Health page warns about the certificate as Panel certificate: 21 days before it expires, as a failure 7 days before, and when getting or renewing it failed. The row links back to this page. Admins also get an email (see Email notifications).

items.title: Real visitor address of the panel
items.text: Only for a panel address behind a CDN or load balancer. See Real visitor address.

items.title: Reboot
items.text: Reboot server… asks you to type the hostname. Every site, the databases and the panel stop until the server is back, usually within one or two minutes. The page waits and reconnects by itself. If the panel does not answer for ten minutes, check the server in your hosting provider's console.

items.title: Audit log
items.text: Each change is in the audit log: system.hostname and system.timezone with the old and the new value, system.reboot with the hostname and whether updates waited for it.

items.title: API and command line
items.text:
Route Scope GET /api/v1/system, GET /api/v1/system/timezones system:read PUT /api/v1/system/hostname, PUT /api/v1/system/timezone system:write POST /api/v1/system/reboot with {"confirm": "<hostname>"} system:write

On the server, as root: hostashi system info, hostashi system timezones, hostashi system timezone ZONE, hostashi system hostname NAME and hostashi system reboot HOSTNAME (see Command line).

items.title: Requirements
items.text: The agent talks to systemd-timedated, systemd-hostnamed and systemd-logind over the system bus. The installer adds the dbus and tzdata packages. Without a running bus the page says so and changes nothing.

items.title: Users and roles
items.text: For: panel admins.

items.title: Roles
items.text:
Role Sees May admin everything everything, including users, server settings and other admins manager all sites everything about sites, including creating and deleting them; no server settings and no users user only the sites given to them the day-to-day work on those sites, see below

Server settings are only for admins: users, firewall, backups, PHP and Node.js versions, email, system settings, the CloudPanel import and the health checks.

items.title: What a user may do on their sites
items.text:
Allowed Not allowed files, SSH and SFTP keys, cron jobs domains and certificates PHP version and settings changing limits (they can see them) maintenance mode, HSTS letting PHP start programs databases of the site, including import and export own nginx directives restoring a backup of the site disabling or deleting the site

A manager may do the "not allowed" column as well, except own nginx directives, which stay with admins.

A site that is not given to a user is invisible to them: it is not listed, and its address answers as if it did not exist.

items.title: Invite someone
items.text:
1. Open Administration → Users and choose Invite someone.
  2. Enter a user name (3 to 32 characters: lowercase letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore) and the role.
  3. Optionally an email address: the link is sent there if email is set up, and the address becomes the account's once the link is used.
  4. Copy the invitation link and send it. It works once, within 24 hours. The new person sets their own password and, for admins and managers, a second factor.

For the role user, choose which sites the account gets on the account's page. You can change that at any time.

items.title: Second factor
items.text:
Admins and managers always need a second factor (authenticator app or passkey). For users it is optional; you can require it per account under Sign-in.

To require it of every account, turn on Require a second factor for every account in the Second factor box at the bottom of the Users page. The panel first lists the accounts that have none yet. Those accounts can still log in, but only to set one up, and their API tokens stop working until they have. Turning the option off makes it optional for users again; a per-account setting applies again from then on.

items.title: Your own password, authenticator app and passkeys
items.text:
Under Your account → Sign-in and security every account manages its own login:

  • Password: enter the current one and the new one twice. Your other sessions are logged out; the browser you are in stays logged in.
  • Authenticator app (TOTP): set it up, or turn it off with your password and a current code or recovery code. Admins and managers must keep a second factor, so they can turn it off only while they have a passkey.
  • Move to a new device: for a new phone or another app, choose Move to a new device. Enter your password and a current code from the old app, or a recovery code if the old phone is gone. Scan the new QR code and enter the first code of the new app. Until then the old app keeps working. After that, the old app and the old recovery codes stop working, and you get new recovery codes.
  • Passkeys: add one with a name (for example the device), or remove one. A passkey counts as a second factor.

If an email address is set, Hostashi sends a note for each of these changes.

items.title: When someone is locked out
items.text: On the account's page, Reset password and second factor removes both, ends the account's sessions and makes a new invitation link. If you are the last admin and locked out yourself, see Recovery.

items.title: Disable or delete an account
items.text:
Disable ends the account's sessions and stops its API tokens until you enable it again. Delete removes the account and its API tokens for good. The last enabled admin cannot be disabled or deleted, and nobody can change their own role.

Every change to accounts is in the audit log.

items.title: Virus scan
items.text:
The virus scan checks the files of your sites with ClamAV, the open-source scanner from the server's distribution. It finds known malware such as web shells, mailers and infected uploads, lists the files it flagged and lets you move them into a quarantine. It never deletes a file.

A clean result does not mean a clean site: ClamAV finds known samples only. Keep the sites' software up to date and the firewall on.

For: admins switch the scan on for the server. Everybody who can open a site, users too, can scan it and quarantine flagged files. Admins and managers of the site change its schedule, mark false positives and restore files from the quarantine.

items.title: Switch it on
items.text:
The scan is off on a new server. An admin switches it on under System → Virus scan. Hostashi then installs ClamAV and its signature updater from the distribution; that takes a minute or two.

ClamAV needs memory while it scans: plan for about 1.5 GB of free RAM while a site is scanned. The card shows the server's memory and warns below 2 GB. Only one site is scanned at a time on the whole server, so this is paid once, not per site, and it does not count against a site's memory limit. The signatures take about 300 MB on disk and are updated several times a day. ClamAV itself is updated once a day from the distribution: Hostashi updates only the ClamAV packages, also with versions the distribution ships outside its security updates. The card shows the installed version.

Turn off… next to the state removes ClamAV and its signatures again. Findings, the history and the quarantine stay.

You can also install it with the server: install.sh apply --malware-scan (see Install).

items.title: Real-time scan
items.text:
With the virus scan on, an admin can also switch on the Real-time scan under System → Virus scan. ClamAV then watches the sites' homes and checks every file right after it is written or changed, for example an upload through a form, SFTP or the file manager.

The real-time scan only reports. It does not block, move or delete a file: flagged files show up in the site's Security › Virus scan tab as Real time, today, and you quarantine them as usual. Admins get at most one email per site and hour.

It keeps the ClamAV daemon running all the time, so it needs about 1.5 GB of RAM permanently, not only during a scan. Switch it on only on servers with enough memory; the card warns below 4 GB. While it is on, scheduled and manual scans use the daemon too.

Switch real-time scan off stops the daemon and removes its package. Findings stay.

items.title: Scan a site
items.text:
Open the site's Security › Virus scan tab.

  • Scan now scans the site at once, or after the site that is being scanned now.
  • While a scan runs, a bar shows how many files it has read of the files in the site. The server lists the files first ("finding the total"); large files take longer, so the bar can pause.
  • Schedule: weekly (the default), every night, or only on request. Scheduled scans run between 1 and 5 at night, server time, each site at its own fixed time.

ClamAV reads every file in the site's home, read only and without network, as the site's own user. The folder .cache is skipped. Site databases are not scanned.

items.title: Scan some files or folders
items.text:
In the file manager, select up to 100 files and folders and click Scan for viruses. The button is there while the virus scan is on. The scan waits like any other, and its results appear on the Virus scan tab; the history lists the selected paths.

A scan of a selection marks only flagged files inside the selection as gone when they are not there any more. Flagged files elsewhere in the site stay as they are.

items.title: Flagged files
items.text:
Each flagged file shows its path, the name of the signature that matched, its size and when it was first seen. Open folder opens its folder in the file manager.

Action What it does Quarantine Moves the file out of the site, after you confirm. Visitors and the site get a 404 for it. Only a file that is unchanged since the scan is moved. False positive Marks the file as harmless. The same content with the same signature is not reported again, at any path. A changed file is reported again. Restore Puts a quarantined file back where it was, owned by the site's user. It fails if another file is at that path now. Report again Undoes False positive.

A flagged file that is not there in a later scan is listed as gone; Show files that are gone shows those too.

When a scan flags files it had not reported before, admins get an email (see Email notifications).

The Health page lists each site with open findings, and warns when the signatures are older than three days: then freshclam can no longer update them.

items.title: Command line and API
items.text:
Everything on this page is in the API and the command line:

hostashi api malware get-scan
hostashi api malware set-scan on=true
hostashi api malware set-scan realtime=true
hostashi api malware start-site-scan blog
hostashi api malware start-site-scan blog paths=htdocs/wp-content/uploads
hostashi api malware get-site-scan blog
hostashi api malware quarantine-site-finding blog 21

Tokens need the scope malware:read to read, malware:write to scan and act on findings, and malware.engine:write to switch ClamAV on or off.
